stem:
A 27-year-old woman in the emergency department has fever, neck stiffness and photophobia. She is alert, orientated and asking sensible questions. The registrar plans a diagnostic spinal tap once imaging and clotting are satisfactory, and a junior doctor is asked to prepare her.

What must happen before the needle is inserted?

options.A: Proceed on implied consent because suspected meningitis is an emergency
options.B: Have her partner sign the consent form as she is unwell
options.C: Explain why it is needed, what it involves, the significant risks and the alternatives, then obtain her consent
options.D: Describe the steps but leave out the risks so she does not become distressed
options.E: Carry out the procedure now and talk it through with her afterwards

correct_answer: C. Explain why it is needed, what it involves, the significant risks and the alternatives, then obtain her consent
why_correct: She is alert and orientated, so she is presumed to have capacity and her own valid consent is needed before an invasive procedure. Valid consent means she has been told the reason for the test, what it involves, the material risks such as post-procedure headache, bleeding and infection, and the reasonable alternatives. The urgency of possible meningitis does not remove the need for consent when the patient can give it.
why_wrong: A. Implied consent is not enough for an invasive procedure in a patient who can be asked directly. B. Another adult cannot consent on behalf of an adult who has capacity. D. Leaving out material risks makes consent invalid. E. Consent must be obtained before, not after, the procedure.
pearl: Antibiotics should not be delayed for lumbar puncture in suspected bacterial meningitis; consent and the procedure follow, they do not hold up treatment.
thinking: Alert, orientated adult ↓ Capacity is presumed ↓ Invasive procedure needs valid consent ↓ Valid consent needs reason, procedure, material risks and alternatives ↓ Explain fully and obtain her agreement beforehand
exam_trap: A, Implied consent because it is an emergency — urgency feels like a reason to skip the discussion, but the emergency exception applies only when consent cannot be obtained, and she is able to give it.
takeaway: A patient who has capacity must give informed consent before an invasive procedure, even when the clinical situation is urgent.

stem:
On a rehabilitation ward, a 68-year-old man with a recent stroke chooses his own meals, manages his phone and decides who may visit him. A formal assessment shows he cannot grasp or weigh the information needed to decide whether to have a percutaneous gastrostomy. His daughter asks whether this means he can no longer make any decisions for himself.

Which principle answers her question?

options.A: Once incapacity is found for one matter it applies to all his decisions
options.B: His daughter now becomes the decision-maker for all his affairs
options.C: Capacity is judged separately for each decision at the time it needs to be made
options.D: His capacity cannot change, so the result is permanent
options.E: The consultant takes over legal authority for every choice he makes

correct_answer: C. Capacity is judged separately for each decision at the time it needs to be made
why_correct: Under the Mental Capacity Act 2005 capacity is assessed decision by decision and at the time the decision is needed. He lacks capacity for the complex feeding-tube decision but retains it for everyday choices such as meals and visitors, which he continues to make himself. The gastrostomy decision is then made in his best interests.
why_wrong: A. Lacking capacity for one decision says nothing about other decisions. B. A relative has no authority to decide unless they hold a relevant lasting power of attorney or are a court-appointed deputy. D. Capacity can fluctuate and may improve, especially after a stroke, so it should be reassessed. E. The clinician makes the specific best-interests decision about treatment, not every decision in his life.
pearl: Capacity may improve during stroke recovery, so if a decision can safely wait it should be delayed until the person is more likely to be able to make it.
thinking: He makes everyday decisions himself ↓ Cannot understand or weigh the gastrostomy information ↓ Mental Capacity Act: capacity is decision- and time-specific ↓ Lacks capacity for this decision only ↓ He keeps making the other decisions
exam_trap: A, Incapacity applies to all decisions — it seems logical that a failed assessment shows global impairment, but the Act requires a separate judgement for each decision.
takeaway: A person can lack capacity for one decision while keeping it for others, because capacity is decision-specific.

stem:
A 59-year-old builder seen in the GP surgery after a minor heart attack says he will stop his newly started statin and keep smoking, as he would rather enjoy his life than worry about it. He can repeat back the risks the GP has described, explains in his own words why he is choosing this, and has given the same answer at two visits. The GP thinks the choice is very poor.

Which is the most appropriate approach?

options.A: Conclude he lacks capacity because no reasonable person would choose this
options.B: Ask his wife to decide on his behalf
options.C: Accept his decision, as having capacity includes the right to make unwise choices
options.D: Arrange detention so the medication can be given
options.E: Continue the statin without telling him

correct_answer: C. Accept his decision, as having capacity includes the right to make unwise choices
why_correct: He understands, retains and weighs the information and communicates a consistent decision, so he has capacity. The Mental Capacity Act 2005 states that a person must not be treated as lacking capacity merely because they make an unwise decision. The GP should respect his choice, document the discussion and keep the door open for future support, including smoking cessation.
why_wrong: A. An unwise outcome is not evidence of incapacity; the test is about his decision-making process. B. A spouse cannot decide for an adult who has capacity. D. There is no legal basis for detention; the Mental Health Act does not apply to this situation. E. Giving medication covertly to a patient with capacity is unlawful and a breach of trust.
pearl: Capacity is judged on the process of decision-making (understand, retain, use or weigh, communicate), never on whether the outcome is one the clinician agrees with.
thinking: Choice the GP sees as unwise ↓ He understands and retains the risks ↓ Weighs them and gives a consistent answer ↓ Capacity present ↓ Unwise decisions do not prove incapacity ↓ Respect and document
exam_trap: A, Concluding he lacks capacity — a decision that seems irrational invites doubt, but the Act specifically forbids treating someone as lacking capacity merely because a choice is unwise.
takeaway: An adult with capacity may make a decision others consider unwise, and that alone does not show incapacity.

stem:
On the medical ward, a 52-year-old woman with cellulitis spreading up her leg and rising inflammatory markers declines the intravenous antibiotics prescribed for her. The consultant has explained that without them the infection could become life-threatening. She can describe that risk accurately, is fully orientated and has no evidence of mental disorder.

Which response is most appropriate?

options.A: Assess her for detention so the antibiotics can be given
options.B: Give the antibiotics anyway under the doctrine of necessity
options.C: Ask her husband to consent instead
options.D: Discharge her immediately once she signs a self-discharge form
options.E: Respect her refusal while exploring her reasons, confirming she understands the consequences and offering alternatives

correct_answer: E. Respect her refusal while exploring her reasons, confirming she understands the consequences and offering alternatives
why_correct: She has capacity, so her refusal is legally binding even though it may lead to serious harm. Good practice is to explore why she is refusing, make sure she understands what could happen, offer alternatives such as oral treatment, and document the discussion. She should continue to receive other care and be told she can change her mind.
why_wrong: A. The Mental Health Act cannot be used to treat a physical illness in a person with capacity and no mental disorder. B. Necessity applies only when a patient lacks capacity and cannot consent, not to override a valid refusal. C. A spouse cannot consent for an adult who has capacity. D. Refusing one treatment is not a reason to end all care; reasons and alternatives should be explored first.
pearl: A capacitous refusal stands even if it results in death, but the patient should still be offered all other care and alternatives, and the conversation should be revisited.
thinking: Serious infection, treatment declined ↓ Orientated, understands the risk ↓ No mental disorder ↓ Capacity present, so refusal is binding ↓ Explore reasons and offer alternatives ↓ Document and continue other care
exam_trap: B, Doctrine of necessity — the danger to life makes emergency treatment feel justified, but necessity cannot override the refusal of a patient who has capacity.
takeaway: A patient with capacity can refuse even life-saving treatment; respect it while exploring reasons and offering alternatives.

stem:
A 15-year-old girl attends a sexual health clinic alone asking about a contraceptive implant. She explains clearly how it works, its side effects, how long it lasts and what other methods are available, and she has thought about how it fits with her life.

Which concept determines whether she can consent herself?

options.A: Lasting power of attorney
options.B: Advance decision to refuse treatment
options.C: Gillick competence
options.D: Assessment under the Mental Capacity Act as for adults
options.E: Best-interests decision by the clinician

correct_answer: C. Gillick competence
why_correct: A young person under 16 can consent to treatment if they have enough understanding and maturity to fully understand what is proposed, which is known as Gillick competence. She shows a clear grasp of the method, its risks and the alternatives. For contraception specifically, the Fraser guidelines are also applied.
why_wrong: A. A lasting power of attorney is made by an adult for future loss of capacity. B. An advance decision to refuse treatment can only be made by a person aged 18 or over. D. The Mental Capacity Act applies from 16 years, so it is not the governing test for her. E. Best-interests decisions apply when someone lacks capacity, but she appears competent.
pearl: Fraser guidelines are specific to contraception and sexual health advice for under-16s, whereas Gillick competence applies to any treatment decision.
thinking: Age 15, under 16 ↓ Attends alone for treatment ↓ Shows full understanding of method, risks and alternatives ↓ Competence for under-16s is Gillick ↓ She can consent if competent
exam_trap: D, Adult capacity assessment — she is assessed in a similar functional way, but the Mental Capacity Act applies from age 16, so the concept for a 15-year-old is Gillick competence.
takeaway: A child under 16 who fully understands a proposed treatment can consent to it under Gillick competence.
notes: Reviewer fix: why_wrong B: ADRT can only be made by a person aged 18 or over (was 'adults over 18')

stem:
A 38-year-old man with long-standing schizophrenia, stable on depot antipsychotic, is told by the surgical team that he needs a laparoscopic cholecystectomy for recurrent gallstone pain. He declines. He can explain what the operation involves, recalls the risk of further attacks and pancreatitis, says he would rather manage his diet and accept that risk, and gives the same answer the following day.

What is the most appropriate conclusion?

options.A: He has capacity to refuse this operation
options.B: His schizophrenia means he lacks capacity
options.C: Refusing a beneficial operation shows he lacks capacity
options.D: His mother should decide for him
options.E: The team should operate because the benefits outweigh the risks

correct_answer: A. He has capacity to refuse this operation
why_correct: Capacity is assessed for the specific decision, and a mental illness diagnosis does not in itself mean a person lacks capacity. He understands, retains and weighs the information and communicates a stable decision, so he has capacity and his refusal must be respected. The discussion should be documented and the option of surgery kept open.
why_wrong: B. A diagnosis alone never establishes incapacity under the Mental Capacity Act. C. Declining treatment that clinicians recommend is not evidence of incapacity. D. Relatives cannot decide for an adult who has capacity. E. Clinical benefit does not override a valid refusal.
pearl: Before concluding a person lacks capacity, the clinician must show both an impairment of mind or brain and that it causes an inability to make the specific decision.
thinking: Schizophrenia, stable ↓ Understands and recalls the risks ↓ Weighs them against his preference ↓ Consistent decision ↓ Diagnosis does not remove capacity ↓ He has capacity to refuse
exam_trap: B, Schizophrenia means lack of capacity — a psychiatric diagnosis prompts doubt, but the functional test is what matters and he passes every part of it.
takeaway: A mental illness diagnosis does not mean a person lacks capacity; apply the functional test to the decision in hand.

stem:
A 44-year-old professional violinist is listed for an elective carpal tunnel release. During the consent discussion the surgeon covers infection, scarring and persistent symptoms, but does not mention the uncommon risk of nerve injury causing permanent loss of fine finger movement.

What should the surgeon do?

options.A: Leave it out because the complication is rare
options.B: Give her the department leaflet in place of discussing it
options.C: Mention only the risks above a fixed frequency
options.D: Ask a healthcare assistant to cover any remaining risks
options.E: Discuss this risk because it would matter to her in particular

correct_answer: E. Discuss this risk because it would matter to her in particular
why_correct: Following Montgomery, a material risk is one that a reasonable person in the patient's position would consider significant, or that the doctor knows or should know this particular patient would consider significant. Permanent loss of fine finger control is rare but would be devastating for a violinist, so it must be discussed. Reasonable alternatives, including non-surgical management, should also be covered.
why_wrong: A. Rarity does not make a risk immaterial if it would matter to this patient. B. A leaflet supports the discussion but does not replace it. C. Materiality is not defined by a frequency cut-off but by significance to the patient. D. Consent discussions should be held by someone who understands the procedure and its risks.
pearl: GMC guidance asks doctors to find out what matters to the patient so that they can share information about risks of harm the patient would consider significant.
thinking: Elective hand operation ↓ Patient is a violinist ↓ Rare complication would end her career ↓ Montgomery: materiality judged from the patient's perspective ↓ Must discuss this risk and alternatives
exam_trap: A, Leave it out because it is rare — older practice set disclosure by what doctors usually told patients, but Montgomery makes the patient's perspective the test.
takeaway: A risk is material if this particular patient would consider it significant, however uncommon it is.

stem:
In a pre-operative clinic, a 61-year-old retired teacher listed for a total knee replacement is told the reason for the operation, the main complications including infection and blood clots, and the non-surgical options. She asks questions, takes the information home, and later signs the form with no pressure from anyone.

Which concept best describes what has been obtained?

options.A: Implied consent
options.B: A best-interests decision
options.C: Valid informed consent
options.D: Emergency treatment without consent
options.E: A deprivation of liberty authorisation

correct_answer: C. Valid informed consent
why_correct: Valid consent needs three elements: the person has capacity, has been given sufficient information including material risks and alternatives, and agrees voluntarily. She received full information, had time to consider it and agreed freely, so this is valid informed consent. The signed form is evidence of the discussion rather than the consent itself.
why_wrong: A. Implied consent is inferred from actions, such as offering an arm for a blood test, and is not appropriate for major surgery. B. Best-interests decisions are for adults who lack capacity. D. Emergency treatment without consent applies only when consent cannot be obtained. E. Deprivation of liberty safeguards concern restricting the freedom of people who lack capacity.
pearl: A signed consent form does not by itself prove valid consent; what counts is the quality of the discussion, which should be documented.
thinking: Patient has capacity ↓ Given reasons, risks and alternatives ↓ Time to consider and ask questions ↓ Agrees without pressure ↓ Capacity, information and voluntariness all present ↓ Valid informed consent
exam_trap: A, Implied consent — signing after listening may look like simple agreement by conduct, but for major surgery explicit consent after a full discussion is required.
takeaway: Valid consent requires capacity, adequate information and voluntary agreement.

stem:
A 33-year-old man had told the bariatric nurse he did not want gastric bypass surgery. At the next appointment he says he will now go ahead, because his father has said he will stop supporting him financially unless he has the operation. He understands the procedure and its risks well.

What is the main concern about his consent?

options.A: Whether he understands the operation
options.B: Whether he can retain the information
options.C: Whether he has been told about alternatives
options.D: Whether he can communicate his choice
options.E: Whether his consent is given voluntarily

correct_answer: E. Whether his consent is given voluntarily
why_correct: Valid consent must be given freely, without coercion or undue pressure from others. His change of mind followed a financial threat from his father, which raises a real concern that his agreement is not voluntary. The team should speak to him alone, explore his own wishes and make clear that he is free to decline.
why_wrong: A. He understands the procedure well, so understanding is not the problem. B. Nothing suggests he cannot retain information. C. Information about alternatives is not the issue raised by the scenario. D. He is clearly able to state his decision.
pearl: Where pressure from family is suspected, speak to the patient alone and, if needed, give more time before the procedure.
thinking: Previously declined surgery ↓ Changed mind after a financial threat ↓ Understanding and communication intact ↓ Pressure from another person ↓ Voluntariness is in doubt
exam_trap: A, Whether he understands — the consent process often focuses on information, but here his understanding is good and the problem is pressure from his father.
takeaway: Consent obtained under pressure from others may not be valid, because consent must be voluntary.

stem:
A 76-year-old woman with delirium on an orthopaedic ward is told about a proposed hip operation. She explains it back accurately straight away, but within a few minutes has no memory of the conversation and cannot hold the details in mind long enough to reach a decision.

Which part of the capacity test is she failing?

options.A: Retaining the information
options.B: Understanding the information
options.C: Using or weighing the information
options.D: Communicating a decision
options.E: The presumption of capacity

correct_answer: A. Retaining the information
why_correct: The Mental Capacity Act functional test requires a person to understand, retain, use or weigh information, and communicate a decision. She understands it at first but cannot keep it in mind long enough to decide, so retention is impaired. Information only needs to be retained long enough to make the decision, so short retention may still be enough if it allows that.
why_wrong: B. She explains the information back accurately, so she understands it. C. The problem arises before she can weigh anything, because she loses the information. D. Nothing suggests she cannot express a choice. E. The presumption of capacity is a principle of the Act, not one of the functional abilities.
pearl: Delirium often fluctuates, so capacity should be reassessed at a better time of day and information given in short, repeated, written forms to aid retention.
thinking: Explains information accurately ↓ Understanding intact ↓ Forgets within minutes ↓ Cannot keep it long enough to decide ↓ Retention impaired
exam_trap: C, Using or weighing — failing to reach a decision looks like a weighing problem, but she cannot weigh information she has already forgotten.
takeaway: Being unable to retain information long enough to make a decision means failing the retention part of the capacity test.

presentation: Functional test of capacity: using or weighing
stem:
A 47-year-old man with a frontal brain injury is offered a hernia repair. He accurately repeats the procedure and its risks the next day, but when asked to decide he cannot balance any benefit against any risk and changes his answer at random each time he is asked.

Which component of capacity is impaired?

options.A: Understanding the information
options.B: Using or weighing the information
options.C: Retaining the information
options.D: Communicating a decision
options.E: The presumption of capacity

correct_answer: B. Using or weighing the information
why_correct: He understands and remembers the information, but he cannot use it to compare benefits against risks in reaching a decision. This is an impairment of the ability to use or weigh information, which is one of the four functional abilities under the Mental Capacity Act 2005. Frontal lobe injury commonly affects this ability while leaving memory and language intact.
why_wrong: A. He explains the procedure accurately, so understanding is intact. C. He recalls the details the next day, so retention is intact. D. He can state an answer; the problem is how he reaches it. E. The presumption of capacity is a starting principle, not one of the functional abilities.
pearl: People with frontal injury can pass a memory test and talk fluently yet still lack capacity because they cannot weigh information.
thinking: Understands the operation ↓ Remembers it the next day ↓ Cannot balance benefit against risk ↓ Random, shifting answers ↓ Using or weighing impaired
exam_trap: D, Communicating a decision — his answer keeps changing, which looks like a communication problem, but he speaks clearly; the inconsistency comes from being unable to weigh the information.
takeaway: A person who understands and remembers information but cannot balance it to reach a decision fails the using or weighing part of the test.

stem:
A 64-year-old woman with motor neurone disease has lost the ability to speak but uses an eye-gaze communication board. The respiratory team need her decision about starting non-invasive ventilation. She appears to follow the explanation closely and nods appropriately.

Which statement is correct?

options.A: She lacks capacity because she cannot speak
options.B: Her husband should decide on her behalf
options.C: She may have capacity if she can express her decision through her communication aid
options.D: An independent mental capacity advocate should make the decision
options.E: The team should decide in her best interests

correct_answer: C. She may have capacity if she can express her decision through her communication aid
why_correct: Communicating a decision can be done by any means, including writing, signing, gestures or communication aids. The Mental Capacity Act requires all practicable steps to be taken to help a person decide before concluding incapacity. If she can understand, retain and weigh the information and indicate her choice through her eye-gaze board, she has capacity.
why_wrong: A. Loss of speech does not mean loss of capacity if she can communicate another way. B. A spouse has no authority to decide for an adult who has capacity, unless appointed under a relevant lasting power of attorney and she lacks capacity. D. An advocate represents and supports a person but never makes the decision. E. Best-interests decisions apply only if she is shown to lack capacity.
pearl: Speech and language therapists can help assess and support communication in people with speech loss before a capacity judgement is made.
thinking: Cannot speak ↓ Uses an eye-gaze board ↓ Appears to understand ↓ Communication can be by any means ↓ Take all practicable steps ↓ May have capacity
exam_trap: E, Best-interests decision — loss of speech in a serious illness makes the team want to decide for her, but best interests applies only after incapacity is shown, and she may be able to decide.
takeaway: Inability to speak does not mean inability to communicate a decision; support other forms of communication.

stem:
A 71-year-old man with severe vascular dementia on a surgical ward needs a decision about a urinary catheter. He has been assessed as lacking capacity for this decision. He has no lasting power of attorney, no deputy and no advance decision. His nephew, who visits often, says he is next of kin and should make the choice.

Who is responsible for making this decision?

options.A: The clinician proposing the treatment, acting in his best interests after consulting those close to him
options.B: His nephew as next of kin
options.C: An independent mental capacity advocate, who signs the consent
options.D: The hospital clinical ethics committee
options.E: His GP, who has known him longest

correct_answer: A. The clinician proposing the treatment, acting in his best interests after consulting those close to him
why_correct: When an adult lacks capacity and there is no attorney, deputy or valid advance decision, the clinician responsible for the treatment makes the decision in the person's best interests under the Mental Capacity Act 2005. This involves considering his past and present wishes, beliefs and values, and consulting people close to him such as his nephew. Relatives contribute to the decision but do not make it.
why_wrong: B. Being next of kin gives no legal power to consent for another adult. C. An advocate is instructed only when there is nobody appropriate to consult, and supports rather than decides. D. Ethics committees may advise but do not make individual treatment decisions. E. The GP is not responsible for this hospital treatment decision.
pearl: An independent mental capacity advocate must be instructed for serious medical treatment decisions when the person has nobody, other than paid carers, who is appropriate to consult.
thinking: Lacks capacity for this decision ↓ No attorney, deputy or advance decision ↓ Next of kin has no legal authority ↓ Responsible clinician decides ↓ Best interests, after consulting family
exam_trap: B, His nephew as next of kin — relatives are commonly assumed to have authority, but in England and Wales next of kin has no legal power to consent for an adult.
takeaway: Without an attorney or deputy, the responsible clinician makes the decision in the patient's best interests, after consulting those close to them.

stem:
A 79-year-old man with profound deafness is admitted from a care home with a fractured wrist. His hearing aids were left behind, and when the orthopaedic doctor explains the options aloud he looks confused and gives answers unrelated to the questions.

What should the doctor do first?

options.A: Help him communicate, for example with written information or a portable hearing amplifier
options.B: Record that he lacks capacity and treat in his best interests
options.C: Phone his daughter to consent for him
options.D: Proceed with treatment without explanation as it is urgent
options.E: Postpone any treatment until his hearing aids arrive

correct_answer: A. Help him communicate, for example with written information or a portable hearing amplifier
why_correct: Under the Mental Capacity Act 2005 a person must not be treated as unable to make a decision until all practicable steps to help them have been taken without success. His confusion is likely caused by the communication barrier, not by an inability to decide. Written explanations, a portable amplifier or other communication support should be used before capacity is judged.
why_wrong: B. Incapacity cannot be concluded until practicable steps to support communication have been tried. C. A relative cannot consent for an adult unless they hold relevant legal authority. D. The injury is not so urgent that his involvement can be bypassed. E. Waiting for hearing aids delays care when other ways of communicating are available now.
pearl: The second principle of the Mental Capacity Act is that all practicable steps must be taken to help someone make a decision before they are treated as unable to.
thinking: Apparent confusion ↓ Profound deafness, no hearing aids ↓ Communication barrier, not necessarily incapacity ↓ Take all practicable steps ↓ Support communication first
exam_trap: B, Record that he lacks capacity — his muddled answers look like cognitive impairment, but incapacity cannot be concluded before his hearing problem has been addressed.
takeaway: Support a person's communication and understanding before deciding they lack capacity.
notes: Reviewer fix: Option A: removed sign language interpreter (hearing-aid user, not a signer); correct_answer and why_correct synced

stem:
An 84-year-old woman from a care home is admitted with a chest infection. Her notes record Alzheimer's disease. She keeps walking towards the exit, and when the doctor explains that she needs intravenous antibiotics, she does not seem to follow why.

Which principle should guide whether she can decide about this treatment?

options.A: She lacks capacity because she has dementia
options.B: She has capacity simply because she is an adult
options.C: Her children should decide about all her treatment
options.D: Assess her capacity for this specific treatment decision now
options.E: Delay any capacity assessment until she is back at the care home

correct_answer: D. Assess her capacity for this specific treatment decision now
why_correct: Capacity is decision-specific and must be assessed when the decision needs to be made, using the functional test of understanding, retaining, using or weighing information and communicating a choice. Dementia raises concern but does not on its own show incapacity. If she is found to lack capacity for this decision, treatment is given in her best interests.
why_wrong: A. A diagnosis of dementia alone does not establish incapacity. B. Capacity is presumed, but the presumption can be rebutted after assessment when there is reason to doubt it, as here. C. Relatives have no automatic authority unless they hold a relevant lasting power of attorney. E. The decision is needed now, so capacity must be assessed now.
pearl: Attempts to leave the ward by someone who lacks capacity may also raise deprivation of liberty considerations, which need separate authorisation.
thinking: Dementia and possible confusion ↓ Reason to doubt capacity ↓ Diagnosis alone is not enough ↓ Assess for this decision at this time ↓ Best interests if lacking
exam_trap: A, She lacks capacity because of dementia — the diagnosis and wandering make incapacity seem obvious, but the Act requires a decision-specific functional assessment.
takeaway: Assess capacity for the specific decision at the time it is needed, rather than assuming it from a diagnosis.

stem:
On a care home visit, a GP is asked to see Dorothy, 88, who has moderate Alzheimer disease. The podiatrist recommends removal of an infected ingrowing toenail under local anaesthetic and wants to know whether she can agree to it herself. Her daughter is happy for it to go ahead.

Which of the following should the GP base the judgement on?

options.A: Her score on a standard cognitive screening questionnaire
options.B: Whether her daughter supports the plan
options.C: Whether she is oriented to time, place and person
options.D: Her ability to understand, retain and use or weigh the information about the procedure and to communicate her decision
options.E: Whether she accepts the podiatrist's advice

correct_answer: D. Her ability to understand, retain and use or weigh the information about the procedure and to communicate her decision
why_correct: The Mental Capacity Act 2005 uses a two-stage, decision-specific test. Once an impairment of mind or brain is present, the question is whether she can understand the information relevant to this procedure, retain it long enough, use or weigh it, and communicate a choice. Dementia alone does not answer that question, so the GP must test these abilities for this toenail decision.
why_wrong: A. A screening score measures global cognition and cannot settle capacity for a particular decision. B. A relative's view does not determine whether the patient herself has capacity. C. Disorientation does not by itself show she cannot understand this specific choice. E. A capacitous person may make a decision others disagree with, so agreement is irrelevant.
pearl: Under the Mental Capacity Act, if a person fails any one of the four functional abilities (understand, retain, use or weigh, communicate), she lacks capacity for that decision at that time.
thinking: Decision needed about a minor procedure ↓ Impairment present (dementia) but this does not decide capacity ↓ Apply the functional test to this decision ↓ Understand, retain, use or weigh, communicate ↓ Base judgement on those abilities
exam_trap: A, A cognitive screening score — it feels objective and quick, but no score threshold defines capacity; the functional test for the specific decision does.
takeaway: Capacity is judged by the four functional abilities for the decision in hand, not by a diagnosis, a score or the family's view.

stem:
Six months ago a hospital doctor recorded that Arthur, a 79-year-old man with vascular dementia, lacked capacity to manage his finances. He is now on a surgical ward and needs a decision about an elective hernia repair. The ward nurse suggests the earlier assessment can simply be applied.

Which statement best reflects the law on mental capacity?

options.A: The earlier finding of incapacity applies to all later decisions
options.B: Capacity must be assessed for the hernia decision at the time it needs to be made
options.C: His wife becomes the decision-maker now that dementia is established
options.D: A diagnosis of vascular dementia means he cannot consent to surgery
options.E: A cognitive test score below a set threshold confirms he lacks capacity

correct_answer: B. Capacity must be assessed for the hernia decision at the time it needs to be made
why_correct: The Mental Capacity Act 2005 treats capacity as specific to each decision and to the time it is made. Lacking capacity for complex finances does not mean he lacks capacity to decide about a hernia repair now, so a fresh assessment for this decision is required.
why_wrong: A. An earlier assessment for a different decision cannot be transferred, and capacity can change over time. C. A spouse has no authority to decide unless appointed under a relevant lasting power of attorney. D. A diagnosis never by itself establishes incapacity. E. No test score defines capacity; the functional test does.
pearl: Every adult is presumed to have capacity, and all practicable steps to help the person decide must be taken before concluding otherwise.
thinking: Previous assessment was for finances ↓ New decision is about surgery ↓ Capacity is decision-specific and time-specific ↓ Diagnosis and old findings do not transfer ↓ Reassess for this decision now
exam_trap: A, Relying on the earlier finding — it seems efficient and documented, but capacity for one decision at one time says nothing reliable about a different decision later.
takeaway: Assess capacity afresh for each decision, at the time it needs to be made.

presentation: Gillick competence for sexual health treatment
stem:
At a sexual health clinic, Kayla, aged 14, attends alone with vaginal discharge after unprotected sex with her boyfriend of similar age. Swabs confirm chlamydia. She explains clearly what the infection is, why antibiotics are needed and what would happen if it went untreated, and she does not want her mother told. Safeguarding questions raise no concerns.

What principle governs whether she can agree to treatment?

options.A: She may have the swabs but treatment must wait for parental agreement
options.B: A young person under 16 with sufficient understanding and maturity can consent to her own treatment
options.C: She can be treated only if her mother is informed afterwards
options.D: The clinician should decide treatment in her best interests as she is a minor
options.E: Consent is not valid until she reaches 16 years of age

correct_answer: B. A young person under 16 with sufficient understanding and maturity can consent to her own treatment
why_correct: Under Gillick competence, a young person under 16 who has enough understanding and intelligence to grasp what is proposed and its implications can give valid consent. Kayla shows this, so she can consent to antibiotic treatment herself, and the Fraser guidance supports confidential sexual health care while encouraging her to involve a parent.
why_wrong: A. A competent young person can consent to treatment, not just to tests. C. Confidentiality should be respected unless there is a safeguarding concern; informing her mother is not a condition of consent. D. Best-interests decisions are for those who lack capacity, and she is competent. E. Age 16 is not a fixed bar when a younger person is Gillick competent.
pearl: A sexual health consultation with an under-16 should always include a safeguarding assessment, and sexual activity in a child under 13 is always a safeguarding referral.
thinking: Age 14, attending alone ↓ Understands diagnosis, treatment and consequences ↓ Gillick competent ↓ Can consent to her own treatment ↓ Encourage, but do not require, parental involvement
exam_trap: E, Waiting until she is 16 — it reflects the age at which consent is presumed, but under-16s can consent when they are competent.
takeaway: A competent under-16 can consent to her own treatment without a parent's agreement.

stem:
A 58-year-old retired teacher is offered a coronary angiogram after an abnormal stress test. Before agreeing, she asks the cardiology registrar in outpatients to go through what could go wrong, how likely each problem is, and what alternatives exist if she says no. She has no cognitive impairment.

Which principle should guide the registrar's response?

options.A: Withholding upsetting risks to avoid causing anxiety
options.B: Acting in her best interests as judged by the clinician
options.C: Shared decision-making leading to informed consent
options.D: Openness after an adverse event has occurred
options.E: Protecting confidential information from disclosure

correct_answer: C. Shared decision-making leading to informed consent
why_correct: She has capacity and is asking for the information she needs to decide. GMC guidance on decision-making and consent, and the Montgomery ruling, require doctors to discuss risks that are material to her and the reasonable alternatives, including doing nothing, and to reach the decision together.
why_wrong: A. Withholding information is justified only in exceptional circumstances of serious harm, not to spare anxiety, and conflicts with her request. B. Best-interests decisions apply only when a patient lacks capacity. D. That describes the duty of candour after something goes wrong. E. Confidentiality is not the issue in this conversation.
pearl: A risk is material if a reasonable person in the patient's position would attach significance to it, or if the doctor knows this particular patient would.
thinking: Patient has capacity ↓ She asks about risks and alternatives ↓ Decision belongs to her ↓ Share relevant information and options ↓ Shared decision-making and informed consent
exam_trap: A, Withholding upsetting risks — it may feel kind, but the so-called therapeutic exception is very narrow and cannot be used simply to avoid distress.
takeaway: A capacitous patient should receive the information she needs and make the decision in partnership with the doctor.

stem:
Overnight on a medical ward, an 82-year-old man admitted with a urinary tract infection becomes agitated and disorientated. Normally he lives independently and manages his own affairs. He now pulls out his cannula and cannot hold onto an explanation of why intravenous antibiotics are needed for more than a few moments. Nobody holds lasting power of attorney for him.

What is the most appropriate approach?

options.A: Use the Mental Health Act to give the antibiotics
options.B: Accept his refusal because he is an adult
options.C: Assess his capacity for this decision and, if lacking, give treatment in his best interests
options.D: Ask his son to sign consent for the antibiotics
options.E: Withhold antibiotics until the confusion settles

correct_answer: C. Assess his capacity for this decision and, if lacking, give treatment in his best interests
why_correct: Delirium can temporarily remove capacity. He cannot retain the information, so on assessment he lacks capacity for this decision now. Under the Mental Capacity Act, necessary treatment that cannot wait can be given in his best interests, using the least restrictive option, and capacity should be reassessed as the delirium improves.
why_wrong: A. The Mental Health Act authorises treatment for mental disorder, not antibiotics for a physical infection. B. The presumption of capacity is rebutted when he cannot retain the information. D. A relative cannot consent for an adult without legal authority such as a lasting power of attorney. E. Delaying treatment of infection would risk harm and may worsen the delirium.
pearl: When capacity is likely to return, consider whether the decision can wait; if it cannot, act in best interests and reassess regularly.
thinking: Previously capacitous adult ↓ Acute delirium from infection ↓ Cannot retain information, so lacks capacity now ↓ Treatment cannot safely wait ↓ Best-interests treatment under the Mental Capacity Act
exam_trap: A, The Mental Health Act — confusion sounds like a mental health issue, but the Act does not cover treating a physical illness such as infection.
takeaway: In fluctuating capacity, assess for the decision now and treat urgent problems in the patient's best interests.

stem:
While writing the discharge summary, a foundation doctor notices that a handwritten ward round entry from yesterday records the wrong side for a patient's leg ulcer. The entry is in the paper notes.

How should the mistake be put right?

options.A: Use correction fluid over the mistake and rewrite the line
options.B: Take out the page and rewrite the entry on a new sheet
options.C: Strike through the error once so it stays legible and add a signed, dated correction
options.D: Ask a colleague to rewrite the entry without referring to the mistake
options.E: Discard the existing notes and open a fresh set

correct_answer: C. Strike through the error once so it stays legible and add a signed, dated correction
why_correct: Clinical records must be accurate and auditable. A correction should leave the original entry legible, with a clear amendment showing who made it and when, so that anyone reading the notes can see what was changed and why.
why_wrong: A. Obliterating the original removes the audit trail and can look like concealment. B. Removing pages destroys part of the record. D. Rewriting without acknowledging the error is dishonest and hides it. E. Records must be kept, not destroyed and replaced.
pearl: Altering records to conceal an error is a serious probity issue that can lead to GMC fitness to practise proceedings.
thinking: Error found in paper notes ↓ Record must remain auditable ↓ Original must remain visible ↓ Add dated, timed and signed correction ↓ Single-line strike-through and amendment
exam_trap: B, Replacing the page — it gives a neat, correct record, but it removes the original entry and breaks the audit trail.
takeaway: Correct a record openly: strike through once, keep it legible, and sign and date the amendment.
notes: Reviewer fix: Shortened keyed option C, which was much longer and more detailed than the distractors (length cue)

stem:
A GP registrar in a busy practice asks the practice healthcare assistant to perform phlebotomy and an ECG on a patient with suspected angina, so that the registrar can see other patients.

What is the registrar still responsible for?

options.A: Staying present for the whole of each task
options.B: Making sure the assistant has a doctor's qualifications
options.C: Getting the patient's written consent to the tasks being delegated
options.D: Nothing further, as accountability passes fully to the assistant
options.E: Being satisfied that the assistant is competent to carry out the tasks

correct_answer: E. Being satisfied that the assistant is competent to carry out the tasks
why_correct: GMC guidance says that when you delegate, you remain responsible for the decision to delegate. The registrar must be satisfied that the assistant has the knowledge, skills and experience for these tasks, give clear instructions, and make sure the results come back for review.
why_wrong: A. Continuous supervision is not needed when the person is competent for the task. B. The person needs competence for the specific task, not the same qualifications. C. Separate written consent to delegation is not required. D. The doctor remains responsible for the overall care and for the decision to delegate.
pearl: Delegation and referral differ: in referral, responsibility for the patient's care is transferred in part or in full, whereas in delegation the doctor keeps responsibility for the overall management.
thinking: Task handed to another professional ↓ This is delegation, not referral ↓ Doctor keeps responsibility for the decision to delegate ↓ Must check competence and give clear instructions ↓ Ensure competence
exam_trap: D, Accountability passes to the assistant — it seems logical that the person doing the task owns it, but the doctor stays responsible for choosing to delegate and for the patient's overall care.
takeaway: When delegating, make sure the person is competent for the task; you remain responsible for that decision.

stem:
At 2 am a foundation doctor is called to a 66-year-old woman two days after a bowel resection. Her early warning score has risen sharply over the last two hours: she is tachycardic, her blood pressure has fallen and she seems drowsier. The doctor cannot work out whether this is bleeding, sepsis or something else.

What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Leave a note for the morning team to review her
options.B: Send blood tests and decide what to do once results are back
options.C: Write up the findings and return to the other ward jobs
options.D: Call the surgical registrar now and request urgent senior review
options.E: Increase observations to hourly and reassess in four hours

correct_answer: D. Call the surgical registrar now and request urgent senior review
why_correct: A sharply rising early warning score with shock signs needs urgent senior input whatever the cause. Escalation does not depend on knowing the diagnosis, and the foundation doctor should start initial management while contacting the registrar, following the local escalation protocol.
why_wrong: A. Waiting until morning risks avoidable harm in a patient who may be bleeding or septic. B. Tests are useful, but waiting for results before escalating delays treatment. C. Documentation alone does not respond to the deterioration. E. More frequent observations without senior review does not address the problem.
pearl: NEWS2 guidance links rising scores to an escalating response, with a high score requiring emergency assessment by a team with critical care competencies.
thinking: Rising early warning score after surgery ↓ Shock signs present ↓ Cause uncertain ↓ Uncertainty is not a reason to wait ↓ Escalate to a senior now
exam_trap: E, Increasing the observation frequency — it feels like closer monitoring, but it watches the deterioration without anyone acting on it.
takeaway: Escalate a deteriorating patient promptly; a diagnosis is not needed first.

stem:
A first-year foundation doctor covering the respiratory ward is asked to review a 71-year-old man with known COPD whose oxygen saturation keeps dropping despite nebulisers and steroids. A blood gas shows worsening hypercapnic acidosis and the doctor recognises he may need non-invasive ventilation, which the doctor has never set up or prescribed.

What should the doctor do?

options.A: Leave the plan for the consultant ward round
options.B: Set up non-invasive ventilation alone using an online guide
options.C: Increase the oxygen to high flow and reassess later
options.D: Contact the medical registrar promptly for senior help
options.E: Repeat the nebulisers and recheck the blood gas tomorrow

correct_answer: D. Contact the medical registrar promptly for senior help
why_correct: The doctor has recognised the likely problem but the next step is beyond their competence. GMC guidance requires doctors to work within their competence and seek help when needed, so prompt escalation to the medical registrar is right, as this man is deteriorating and needs an urgent decision about ventilatory support.
why_wrong: A. Waiting for the ward round delays treatment in a patient getting worse. B. Starting a treatment you are not trained to give puts the patient at risk. C. High-flow oxygen may worsen hypercapnia in COPD and does not secure senior help. E. Deferring reassessment to the next day is unsafe in worsening acidosis.
pearl: In COPD patients at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure, oxygen is titrated to a target saturation of 88 to 92 percent.
thinking: Patient deteriorating despite initial treatment ↓ Doctor recognises likely need for NIV ↓ Task is beyond the doctor's competence ↓ Delay is unsafe ↓ Seek senior help promptly
exam_trap: B, Setting it up alone — it seems proactive, but acting beyond your competence without supervision can harm the patient.
takeaway: Recognise the limits of your competence and seek senior help promptly for a deteriorating patient.

presentation: Persistent escalation when concerns are not acted on
stem:
A foundation doctor on a surgical ward bleeps the on-call registrar about a 54-year-old man with suspected anastomotic leak who is becoming more tachycardic and hypotensive. The registrar, busy in theatre, says they will come when they can. An hour later the patient is worse and still has not been seen.

What should the foundation doctor do next?

options.A: Escalate further, for example to the on-call consultant or the critical care outreach team
options.B: Move the patient to another ward where a team might see him
options.C: Record the earlier call in the notes and keep waiting
options.D: Carry on hourly observations until the registrar arrives
options.E: Ask the morning consultant ward round to review him

correct_answer: A. Escalate further, for example to the on-call consultant or the critical care outreach team
why_correct: If a deteriorating patient is not being reviewed, the doctor must keep escalating through the hierarchy until appropriate help arrives, for example to the consultant or the outreach team, and should document each step. Patient safety comes before concern about bypassing a busy senior.
why_wrong: B. Moving him does not secure senior review and may delay it. C. Documentation without further action leaves him at risk. D. Observations alone do not bring the review he needs. E. Waiting until morning could allow avoidable harm.
pearl: Most hospitals have a critical care outreach or rapid response team that can be called directly for a deteriorating patient, whatever the grade of the caller.
thinking: Deteriorating patient escalated once ↓ Senior unavailable and patient worse ↓ Initial escalation has failed ↓ Duty to persist ↓ Escalate higher and document
exam_trap: C, Documenting and waiting — it creates a record that you raised the concern, but it leaves the patient unreviewed while getting worse.
takeaway: If the first escalation does not produce a review, keep escalating until help arrives.

stem:
A man in his forties has been kept waiting at his GP surgery well beyond his appointment time. When he is finally called in, he speaks loudly and complains that nobody told him about the delay, but he is not threatening and makes no aggressive gestures.

What is the most appropriate way for the GP to respond?

options.A: Tell him the delay was caused by other patients and is not the GP's fault
options.B: Call the police to report disruptive behaviour
options.C: Ask the practice manager to remove him from the premises
options.D: Match his volume so that he stops interrupting
options.E: Stay calm, listen and acknowledge his frustration about the wait

correct_answer: E. Stay calm, listen and acknowledge his frustration about the wait
why_correct: He is frustrated but not threatening. A calm tone, active listening and acknowledging his concern, often with an apology for the wait, are the most effective ways to de-escalate and allow the consultation to continue.
why_wrong: A. Deflecting blame dismisses his concern and may inflame things. B. Police involvement is disproportionate when there is no threat. C. Removing him is disproportionate for verbal frustration. D. Raising your own voice is likely to escalate the situation.
pearl: If anger does escalate to threats or violence, the priority becomes personal and staff safety: leave the room, use the alarm and seek help.
thinking: Patient angry about a delay ↓ No threat or violence ↓ Aim is to de-escalate ↓ Calm tone, listen, acknowledge ↓ Continue the consultation
exam_trap: A, Explaining that it is not the GP's fault — it may be true, but it sounds defensive and ignores what he is feeling.
takeaway: Calm listening and acknowledgement defuse most verbal anger.

presentation: Disclosure of domestic abuse with a request for secrecy
stem:
During a smear test appointment, a 34-year-old woman tells the GP that her husband hit her last week and has done so before. She says she does not want anyone else to know. There are no children in the household.

What is the most appropriate initial response by the GP?

options.A: Leave the disclosure out of her notes as she requested
options.B: Report the assault to the police immediately despite her wishes
options.C: Suggest she brings her husband to the next appointment to talk it through
options.D: Listen supportively, assess her current safety and discuss sources of support
options.E: Tell her she must move out of the house as soon as possible

correct_answer: D. Listen supportively, assess her current safety and discuss sources of support
why_correct: A disclosure of domestic abuse needs a non-judgemental response, an assessment of immediate risk, explanation of the limits of confidentiality, and signposting or referral to specialist domestic abuse services, in line with NICE guidance. She is a capacitous adult and her wishes should usually be respected unless there is a serious risk to her or others.
why_wrong: A. The disclosure should be recorded confidentially, as it is important for her safety and future care. B. Sharing without consent is not the first step for a capacitous adult unless there is serious risk to others or a high risk of serious harm. C. Involving the abuser may put her at greater risk. E. Directing her to leave ignores her autonomy, and leaving without a plan can be the most dangerous time.
pearl: A risk assessment tool such as DASH helps identify high-risk victims, who may be referred to a multi-agency risk assessment conference.
thinking: Adult discloses partner violence ↓ Asks for confidentiality ↓ Listen without judgement ↓ Assess immediate risk and explain confidentiality limits ↓ Document and offer specialist support
exam_trap: A, Not recording it — it seems to respect her request, but documentation is needed for her safety and continuity, and it stays confidential within the record.
takeaway: Respond to a domestic abuse disclosure supportively, assess risk, document it, and offer specialist help.

stem:
A 26-year-old woman attends the antenatal clinic at 20 weeks with bruising on her forearm that she says came from walking into a door. Her husband stays in the room, answers questions on her behalf and declines to step out when the midwife asks.

What should the clinician aim to do?

options.A: Accept the husband's account and complete the appointment
options.B: Discuss her sensitive history in front of her husband as he is family
options.C: Find a way to see her alone, such as during a routine urine sample or examination
options.D: Decline to continue the appointment until he leaves
options.E: Tell the husband that the bruise suggests abuse

correct_answer: C. Find a way to see her alone, such as during a routine urine sample or examination
why_correct: A partner who will not leave and answers for the patient is a recognised warning sign of domestic abuse. UK antenatal guidance advises that every pregnant woman is seen alone for at least part of one appointment, so the clinician should create a safe opportunity to speak with her privately and ask directly.
why_wrong: A. Accepting his account may miss abuse. B. Sensitive matters should not be discussed in front of another person without her agreement. D. Refusing care harms her and her baby. E. Confronting the partner may increase the danger to her.
pearl: Domestic abuse often starts or escalates during pregnancy, so routine enquiry should be made when the woman is seen alone.
thinking: Partner refuses to leave and speaks for her ↓ Unexplained injury in pregnancy ↓ Possible domestic abuse ↓ She cannot disclose with him present ↓ Arrange private time safely
exam_trap: D, Refusing to continue — it seems to put pressure on the partner, but it denies her care and may close off the chance to help her.
takeaway: When a partner dominates a consultation, find a safe way to see the patient alone.
notes: Reviewer fix: Softened unverifiable 'NICE advises at least one appointment alone' attribution to UK antenatal guidance wording

stem:
In the hospice day unit, a 63-year-old man with metastatic pancreatic cancer who has stopped chemotherapy asks the palliative care doctor directly whether he will see his granddaughter's wedding in eight months.

What is the best way for the doctor to respond?

options.A: Find out what he wants to know and give an honest estimate with its uncertainty
options.B: Promise him that he will certainly be there
options.C: Tell him he has exactly two months
options.D: Suggest it is better not to think about time at the moment
options.E: Speak to his wife about the outlook before answering him

correct_answer: A. Find out what he wants to know and give an honest estimate with its uncertainty
why_correct: Good communication about prognosis starts by exploring what the patient already understands and how much he wants to know, then giving honest information in ranges, such as weeks to months, and acknowledging uncertainty. This lets him plan for what matters to him.
why_wrong: B. False reassurance is dishonest and stops him planning. C. A precise figure is rarely accurate and can mislead. D. Deflecting the question denies him information he has asked for. E. Information about a capacitous patient should not be shared with family before him without his consent.
pearl: Prognosis is best given in time ranges with honest uncertainty, and it can be revisited as his condition changes.
thinking: Patient asks about prognosis ↓ Explore his understanding and wishes ↓ Be honest without false precision ↓ Acknowledge uncertainty ↓ Support planning
exam_trap: D, Discouraging thoughts about time — it may seem kind, but it avoids his direct question and prevents him planning his remaining time.
takeaway: Ask what the patient wants to know, then answer honestly with uncertainty acknowledged.

presentation: Duty of candour after harmful error
stem:
Two days after a hip replacement, a 71-year-old man on the orthopaedic ward develops a large wound haematoma and has to return to theatre. Reviewing his drug chart, the FY2 doctor finds that a transcription mistake led to his anticoagulant injection being given twice on the same evening. When the FY2 visits, the man asks directly whether something went wrong with his care.

What is the most appropriate response?

options.A: Tell him nothing can be said until the formal incident investigation has concluded
options.B: Acknowledge that a mistake occurred, apologise, explain what happened and what will be done now
options.C: Explain that bleeding is a known risk of joint replacement surgery
options.D: Explain that the nursing team was responsible for giving the extra dose
options.E: Talk it through openly with him but leave the conversation out of the notes

correct_answer: B. Acknowledge that a mistake occurred, apologise, explain what happened and what will be done now
why_correct: He has been harmed by an error and is asking about it directly, so the professional duty of candour applies. He should be told promptly and honestly what happened, receive a sincere apology, and be told what is being done to put things right and prevent a recurrence. An apology is not an admission of legal liability, and the conversation should be documented and the incident reported.
why_wrong: A. A pending investigation does not justify withholding the basic facts; the patient should be told promptly and updated as findings emerge. C. Presenting an error as a recognised complication is misleading and breaches candour. D. Blaming colleagues misrepresents what is known and is unprofessional; the system failure is investigated through incident reporting. E. Significant conversations about harm must be recorded in the clinical notes.
pearl: Saying sorry is not an admission of liability, and NHS Resolution encourages early apology when things go wrong.
thinking: Patient harmed: return to theatre ↓ Cause is a medication error, not a recognised complication ↓ Patient asks directly ↓ Duty of candour: open, honest, timely ↓ Explain, apologise, outline next steps, document and report
exam_trap: A, Waiting for the investigation — it feels cautious and fair to staff, but candour requires timely disclosure of what is known now, with updates later.
takeaway: When an error has harmed a patient, tell them honestly and promptly, apologise and explain what happens next.

stem:
A 19-year-old man is rushed into the emergency department by ambulance after eating a dessert containing peanuts. He has noisy inspiratory stridor, swollen lips and tongue, and is too drowsy and breathless to speak. No family members are with him and his phone is locked.

Which principle should guide the team's immediate actions?

options.A: Wait until his parents can be contacted to give permission
options.B: Give immediate life-saving treatment in his best interests without delay
options.C: Obtain signed consent from a relative by telephone before treating
options.D: Defer treatment until he is well enough to discuss the risks and benefits
options.E: Apply urgently to the Court of Protection for authorisation

correct_answer: B. Give immediate life-saving treatment in his best interests without delay
why_correct: He has a life-threatening airway problem from anaphylaxis and cannot currently take part in decisions. When delay would risk death or serious harm and there is no known valid refusal, clinicians should provide the treatment immediately necessary in the patient's best interests. Consent processes must never hold up life-saving care such as intramuscular adrenaline and airway support.
why_wrong: A. Relatives cannot consent for an adult, and waiting would be dangerous. C. There is no requirement for written consent, and a relative's signature has no legal authority for an adult. D. Delaying until he can discuss treatment could be fatal. E. Court involvement is for disputed, non-urgent decisions, not for emergencies.
pearl: Emergency treatment without consent should be limited to what is immediately necessary; decisions that can wait should be left until the patient can take part.
thinking: Stridor and drowsiness: imminent airway compromise ↓ Unable to give or refuse consent ↓ No known advance refusal ↓ Delay risks death ↓ Treat immediately in his best interests
exam_trap: A, Waiting for his parents — involving family feels respectful, but they cannot consent for an adult and any delay could cost his life.
takeaway: In a life-threatening emergency, give the necessary treatment immediately in the patient's best interests.

presentation: Valid advance decision to refuse antibiotics
stem:
An 82-year-old man with advanced Parkinson's disease is sent from his care home to hospital, unresponsive and febrile with right lower lobe pneumonia. His keyworker brings a document he wrote two years ago while he had capacity. It is signed and witnessed, refuses intravenous antibiotics for any chest infection, and states that this applies even if his life is at risk. His daughter pleads with the medical team to start antibiotics.

Which principle should guide management?

options.A: The advance decision is valid and applicable, so intravenous antibiotics should not be given
options.B: The document no longer has effect now that he is unconscious
options.C: His daughter, as next of kin, can overrule the document
options.D: The document means that all care, including comfort measures, should be stopped
options.E: Doctors may disregard the document if they think antibiotics are in his best interests

correct_answer: A. The advance decision is valid and applicable, so intravenous antibiotics should not be given
why_correct: Under the Mental Capacity Act 2005 a valid and applicable advance decision has the same legal effect as a contemporaneous refusal by a person with capacity. Because it concerns life-sustaining treatment, it is in writing, signed, witnessed and states that it applies even if life is at risk. It covers exactly this situation, so the team must not give the refused treatment, while continuing symptom control and comfort care.
why_wrong: B. An advance decision is designed to take effect precisely when the person has lost capacity. C. A relative has no power to override a valid advance decision unless they hold a later lasting power of attorney covering this treatment. D. It refuses only the specified treatment; basic and comfort care must continue. E. Clinicians cannot substitute their view of best interests for a valid, applicable refusal.
pearl: An advance decision cannot demand treatment and cannot refuse basic care such as warmth, hygiene and offering food and drink by mouth.
thinking: Now lacks capacity ↓ Written, signed, witnessed refusal of a specified treatment ↓ States it applies even if life is at risk ↓ Covers the current circumstances ↓ Legally binding: withhold antibiotics, continue comfort care
exam_trap: C, Letting the daughter decide — family distress is powerful, but next of kin has no legal authority to override a valid, applicable advance decision.
takeaway: A valid and applicable advance decision to refuse treatment must be respected even when the patient can no longer speak for themselves.

stem:
At a respiratory clinic, a 68-year-old woman with progressive idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis says she has been thinking about the future. She would like to talk about what should happen if she becomes much more breathless, and mentions that she would prefer not to be admitted to hospital again. She has full capacity.

What is the most appropriate approach?

options.A: Postpone the conversation until her lung function has declined further
options.B: Advise her that her children will make these choices when the time comes
options.C: Explore her wishes and record an advance care plan shared with those involved in her care
options.D: Arrange an elective admission so the inpatient team can discuss it
options.E: Explain that preferences about future care cannot be formally recorded

correct_answer: C. Explore her wishes and record an advance care plan shared with those involved in her care
why_correct: She has a progressive life-limiting illness, has capacity now and is raising the topic herself. Advance care planning lets her discuss and record her values, preferences for place of care and treatment, and any wish to appoint a lasting power of attorney or make an advance decision. Sharing the plan with her GP and out-of-hours services helps ensure her wishes are known if she later loses capacity.
why_wrong: A. Delay risks losing the chance to involve her while she has capacity. B. Relatives cannot make decisions for an adult unless legally appointed, and her own views should be captured now. D. Admission is unnecessary and contrary to her stated wishes. E. Wishes can be recorded in an advance care plan, an advance statement or an advance decision.
pearl: An advance statement of wishes is not legally binding but must be taken into account in any later best-interests decision.
thinking: Life-limiting progressive illness ↓ Patient has capacity and raises the topic ↓ Opportunity for advance care planning ↓ Discuss values, preferences and future options ↓ Document and share the plan
exam_trap: A, Postponing the discussion — waiting can feel kinder, but the opportunity to capture her own wishes may be lost if she deteriorates.
takeaway: When a patient with capacity wants to plan for future care, explore and document their wishes in an advance care plan and share it.

stem:
On a home visit, a GP sees a 75-year-old man with severe heart failure and his wife. Together they talk about where he would like to be cared for in his final weeks, who he would want to speak on his behalf, and which hospital treatments he would or would not want if he became more unwell. They agree to write these preferences down and share them with the out-of-hours service.

Which term best describes this process?

options.A: Advance care planning
options.B: Best interests decision-making
options.C: Mental capacity assessment
options.D: Lasting power of attorney registration
options.E: Significant event analysis

correct_answer: A. Advance care planning
why_correct: Advance care planning is a voluntary process in which a person with capacity discusses and records their values, wishes and priorities for future care, often including preferred place of care and death and who they would like involved. Here the patient himself is making the choices while able to, and the plan is being shared with other services. It may later lead to formal documents, but the discussion itself is advance care planning.
why_wrong: B. Best interests decisions are made for someone who lacks capacity, whereas he is deciding for himself. C. Capacity is presumed and is not the focus of this conversation. D. Naming someone to speak for him may lead to a lasting power of attorney, but registration is a separate legal step with the Office of the Public Guardian. E. Significant event analysis reviews incidents to learn from them.
pearl: Preferences recorded through advance care planning should be shared with GP, ambulance and out-of-hours services, often via an electronic care coordination record.
thinking: Progressive incurable illness ↓ Patient with capacity voicing his own wishes ↓ Covers place of care, spokesperson and treatment limits ↓ Recorded and shared ↓ This is advance care planning
exam_trap: B, Best interests decision-making — the discussion is about future treatment, but best interests applies only when a person lacks capacity, and he is deciding for himself.
takeaway: Discussing and recording a capacitous person's wishes for future care is advance care planning.

stem:
A 79-year-old man with end-stage COPD is admitted to a respiratory ward with an infective exacerbation. After a discussion with him, a DNACPR decision is documented. A newly qualified nurse asks the FY1 doctor whether this means his nebulisers, oxygen and antibiotics should now be stopped.

Which statement about the DNACPR decision is correct?

options.A: It means that active treatment should now be withdrawn
options.B: It means he should be moved onto an end-of-life care pathway
options.C: It rules out escalation to non-invasive ventilation
options.D: It applies only to whether cardiopulmonary resuscitation is attempted
options.E: It means antibiotics should no longer be prescribed

correct_answer: D. It applies only to whether cardiopulmonary resuscitation is attempted
why_correct: A DNACPR decision relates solely to whether cardiopulmonary resuscitation should be attempted if his heart or breathing stops. It does not by itself limit any other treatment, so his nebulisers, oxygen and antibiotics should continue. Other ceilings of care, such as whether to offer ventilatory support, need separate discussion and documentation.
why_wrong: A. Active treatment continues unless separately decided otherwise. B. Many patients with a DNACPR decision are not dying and are expected to recover from the current illness. C. Suitability for non-invasive ventilation is a separate decision. E. Antibiotics remain appropriate for his infection.
pearl: Resuscitation Council UK recommends recording DNACPR decisions within a broader treatment escalation plan, such as ReSPECT, so other ceilings of care are clear.
thinking: DNACPR documented ↓ Question is whether other treatment stops ↓ DNACPR covers CPR only ↓ Other ceilings of care are separate decisions ↓ Continue his current treatment
exam_trap: A, Withdrawing active treatment — a DNACPR order is often misread as 'not for anything', which can lead to dangerous under-treatment.
takeaway: A DNACPR decision concerns only cardiopulmonary resuscitation and does not withdraw other treatment.

presentation: Escalating an unresolved patient safety concern
stem:
An FY1 on a night shift reviews a 54-year-old woman who had a bowel resection yesterday. She has become confused, hypotensive and tachycardic, and her early warning score is climbing. The FY1 telephoned the SHO, who advised repeating observations in two hours, but since then she has deteriorated further.

What should the FY1 do?

options.A: Write the findings in the notes and await the morning ward round
options.B: Submit an incident report and take no further action
options.C: Ask the nurse to repeat the observations in an hour
options.D: Escalate directly to the registrar or critical care outreach, continuing up the chain until she is reviewed
options.E: Raise the situation at the morning handover meeting

correct_answer: D. Escalate directly to the registrar or critical care outreach, continuing up the chain until she is reviewed
why_correct: She has signs of possible sepsis or haemorrhage and is getting worse despite the first escalation. When a safety concern is not acted on, doctors must keep escalating through the hierarchy, to the registrar, consultant or outreach team, until the patient is appropriately reviewed. Patient safety takes priority over reluctance to bypass or challenge a colleague.
why_wrong: A. Waiting hours for a ward round risks avoidable harm. B. Incident reporting is useful afterwards but does not get her reviewed now. C. Repeating observations delays action in a patient already deteriorating. E. Handover is too late for an acutely unwell patient.
pearl: Most hospitals allow any staff member to call the critical care outreach team or a medical emergency team directly if they are worried, regardless of seniority.
thinking: Post-operative patient deteriorating ↓ First escalation did not lead to review ↓ Ongoing risk of serious harm ↓ Duty to escalate further ↓ Registrar or outreach now, then consultant if needed
exam_trap: C, Repeating the observations — it feels like sensible monitoring, but the trend already shows deterioration and further delay only postpones the review she needs.
takeaway: If a concern about a deteriorating patient is not acted on, keep escalating until it is.

stem:
A GP registrar is seeing a 47-year-old man with a new diagnosis of hypertension who also has type 2 diabetes and early kidney disease. She realises she is not sure which antihypertensive is currently recommended first for someone with his combination of conditions.

What is the most appropriate way to decide on treatment?

options.A: Check current national guidance, such as NICE, and apply it with judgement to his individual circumstances
options.B: Prescribe the medicine he would prefer even if there are safety concerns
options.C: Rely on an old textbook from the practice library without checking newer advice
options.D: Follow the guideline rigidly without considering his other conditions
options.E: Make the decision alone without asking colleagues

correct_answer: A. Check current national guidance, such as NICE, and apply it with judgement to his individual circumstances
why_correct: Good practice is to base decisions on current, relevant evidence-based guidance while applying clinical judgement to the individual patient, including comorbidities, preferences and interactions. When unsure, doctors should also feel free to ask senior colleagues. This keeps care safe, up to date and personalised.
why_wrong: B. Patient preference matters but cannot override safety. C. Outdated sources may give recommendations that have since changed. D. Guidelines support but do not replace judgement for individual patients. E. Seeking advice when uncertain is expected and promotes safe care.
pearl: The GMC expects doctors to recognise and work within the limits of their competence and to keep their knowledge up to date.
thinking: Doctor uncertain about best management ↓ Current guidance gives the evidence base ↓ Patient has several conditions ↓ Apply guidance with judgement ↓ Ask colleagues if still unsure
exam_trap: D, Following the guideline rigidly — it seems the safest evidence-based option, but guidelines must be adapted to the individual, especially with comorbidities.
takeaway: Use current evidence-based guidance together with clinical judgement, and ask colleagues when unsure.

presentation: Communicating the limitations of a negative test
stem:
A 62-year-old man returns a home faecal immunochemical test through the bowel cancer screening programme and receives a normal result. He has no bowel symptoms. At a GP appointment for another problem, he asks whether this means he definitely cannot have bowel cancer.

What is the best response?

options.A: Explain that the result makes cancer much less likely but cannot exclude it completely, and describe symptoms that should prompt review
options.B: Reassure him that bowel cancer has now been ruled out
options.C: Arrange a colonoscopy before discussing the result further
options.D: Tell him the result is normal and he will not need further screening
options.E: Advise him to contact the screening hub for an answer
