correct_answer: A. Explain that the result makes cancer much less likely but cannot exclude it completely, and describe symptoms that should prompt review
why_correct: No screening test is perfect, and a normal faecal immunochemical test lowers the probability of bowel cancer without excluding it. Honest explanation of this uncertainty, together with clear safety-netting about rectal bleeding, change in bowel habit, weight loss or other symptoms, lets him make informed decisions and seek help early. He will also be invited again in the next screening round.
why_wrong: B. False reassurance may delay presentation if symptoms develop. C. Colonoscopy is not indicated for an asymptomatic man with a normal result. D. Screening is repeated at regular intervals, so this is incorrect. E. He has asked his own doctor a reasonable question that can be answered now.
pearl: Safety-netting should state which symptoms to look out for, how soon to act and where to seek help.
thinking: Asymptomatic, normal screening result ↓ Asks if cancer is definitely excluded ↓ No test has perfect sensitivity ↓ Be honest about limitations ↓ Safety-net with specific symptoms
exam_trap: B, Saying cancer has been ruled out — it is comforting and matches a normal result, but it overstates the test and can delay presentation later.
takeaway: Be honest about what a test can and cannot exclude, and safety-net clearly.

stem: A 57-year-old woman is seen on the gastroenterology ward after a CT scan for painless jaundice. The report describes a mass in the head of the pancreas that is suspicious for malignancy, and an endoscopic biopsy has been booked. She asks the registrar, 'Does this mean I have cancer?' What is the best way to respond?

options.A: Tell her the mass is most likely a harmless cyst
options.B: Tell her it is cancer so she can begin preparing herself
options.C: Decline to discuss the scan until the biopsy result is available
options.D: Explain honestly that the scan shows a concerning mass, that cancer is possible but not yet confirmed, and what the next steps are
options.E: Tell her the oncologist will explain everything at a later appointment

correct_answer: D. Explain honestly that the scan shows a concerning mass, that cancer is possible but not yet confirmed, and what the next steps are
why_correct: She has asked a direct question and is entitled to an honest answer at a pace that suits her. The registrar should explain what the scan shows, that cancer is a real possibility but the biopsy is needed to confirm it, and what will happen next and when. This avoids both false reassurance and a premature diagnosis, and allows her to ask questions and involve family.
why_wrong: A. False reassurance is dishonest and undermines trust when results return. B. Stating a diagnosis before it is confirmed may be wrong and causes avoidable distress. C. Refusing to discuss known findings leaves her anxious and uninformed. E. Deferring to another clinician avoids a reasonable question the team can answer now.
pearl: Checking what the patient already knows and how much they want to hear before giving information helps tailor difficult conversations.
thinking: Imaging suspicious but not diagnostic ↓ Patient asks directly ↓ Avoid false reassurance and premature diagnosis ↓ Explain known, uncertain and next steps ↓ Offer support and follow-up
exam_trap: C, Waiting for the biopsy — holding back can seem kind, but she already knows something is wrong and silence increases anxiety and erodes trust.
takeaway: When a diagnosis is uncertain, explain what is known, what is not, and what happens next.

stem:
A 48-year-old warehouse operative attends his GP practice two weeks after straining his lower back lifting boxes. He has mechanical pain with no leg symptoms, no neurological signs and no red flag features. He says he cannot manage his usual heavy lifting duties and asks for a note for his employer.

Which approach is most appropriate?

options.A: Refuse a note because simple back pain never justifies time off work
options.B: Request an MRI of the lumbar spine before deciding
options.C: Assess how his symptoms affect his ability to do his job and issue a fit note if justified, considering adjustments
options.D: Sign him off as unfit for any work for six months
options.E: Make an urgent referral to the spinal surgeons

correct_answer: C. Assess how his symptoms affect his ability to do his job and issue a fit note if justified, considering adjustments
why_correct: Fit note decisions should be based on how the condition affects the person's ability to work, not on the diagnosis alone. He may be fit for some work with adjustments such as lighter duties or altered hours, which the 'may be fit for work' option supports, or may need a short period off. Encouraging an early return to suitable activity is also good for recovery from non-specific low back pain.
why_wrong: A. Back pain can genuinely limit work, and a functional assessment is needed rather than a blanket refusal. B. Imaging is not indicated for non-specific low back pain without red flags. D. Long-term complete incapacity is not supported and discourages recovery. E. There is no indication for surgical referral.
pearl: Since 2022 fit notes can also be issued by nurses, pharmacists, physiotherapists and occupational therapists, not only doctors.
thinking: Non-specific low back pain, no red flags ↓ No imaging or specialist referral needed ↓ Fit note depends on function at work ↓ Consider 'may be fit for work' with adjustments ↓ Support early return to activity
exam_trap: B, Requesting an MRI first — it feels thorough, but imaging is not indicated without red flags and is not needed to judge fitness for work.
takeaway: Fit note decisions rest on functional assessment of the person's ability to work, with adjustments considered.

stem:
A 4-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department by her father because she has been crying when her nappy is changed and is not moving her left leg. He cannot recall any fall or injury. A radiograph shows a corner fracture at the distal femoral metaphysis.

What is the significance of this finding?

options.A: It is highly suggestive of non-accidental injury and requires safeguarding referral
options.B: It is a typical accidental fracture in a child of this age
options.C: Rickets is the usual explanation
options.D: Osteogenesis imperfecta is the most likely cause
options.E: It makes abuse unlikely because there is no bruising

correct_answer: A. It is highly suggestive of non-accidental injury and requires safeguarding referral
why_correct: Metaphyseal corner or bucket-handle fractures, the classic metaphyseal lesion, result from forceful twisting or shaking of a limb and are strongly associated with abuse in infants. She is non-mobile and there is no explanation, which adds to the concern. The paediatric team and children's social care should be involved and a skeletal survey and further assessment arranged in line with safeguarding procedures.
why_wrong: B. A non-mobile infant rarely sustains accidental long-bone fractures, and this pattern is not typical of accidental injury. C. Rickets can cause metaphyseal changes but is an uncommon explanation and does not remove the duty to act on safeguarding concerns. D. Osteogenesis imperfecta is rare and still requires investigation alongside safeguarding. E. Bruising is often absent in abusive fractures.
pearl: Any fracture in a non-mobile infant without a clear, consistent explanation should prompt safeguarding assessment.
thinking: Infant, not yet mobile ↓ No history of trauma ↓ Classic metaphyseal lesion on radiograph ↓ Strongly associated with abuse ↓ Safeguarding referral and skeletal survey
exam_trap: D, Osteogenesis imperfecta — bone fragility is a recognised differential, but it is rare and does not explain away the need for a safeguarding response.
takeaway: Metaphyseal fractures in infants are highly suggestive of non-accidental injury and need safeguarding action.

stem:
A 15-year-old boy attends a sexual health clinic asking for condoms and testing for sexually transmitted infections. He has a girlfriend of the same age, understands the advice given and is judged competent. There are no safeguarding concerns. His mother is in the waiting room and he asks that she is not told why he came.

What is the most appropriate approach?

options.A: Inform his mother, because he is under 16
options.B: Ask him to return with a parent before giving any advice
options.C: Refuse sexual health advice until he turns 16
options.D: Obtain written permission from his school first
options.E: Keep the consultation confidential, while explaining the limited circumstances in which information might need to be shared

correct_answer: E. Keep the consultation confidential, while explaining the limited circumstances in which information might need to be shared
why_correct: A competent young person under 16 is owed the same duty of confidentiality as an adult. With no safeguarding concerns, his request should be respected, while explaining that information may be shared if there were a risk of serious harm to him or others. He can be encouraged, but not required, to involve a parent.
why_wrong: A. Being under 16 does not remove the right to confidentiality for a competent young person. B. Insisting on a parent may deter him from seeking care. C. Withholding sexual health advice risks harm to his health. D. Schools have no role in authorising his care.
pearl: Sexual activity involving a child under 13 always requires safeguarding referral, as a child of that age cannot legally consent.
thinking: Under 16 but competent ↓ No safeguarding concerns ↓ Requests confidentiality ↓ Duty of confidentiality applies ↓ Respect it, explain limits, encourage parental involvement
exam_trap: A, Telling his mother — it feels protective because of his age, but there is no justification for breaching a competent young person's confidence.
takeaway: A competent under-16 is owed confidentiality unless there is a risk of serious harm that justifies disclosure.

stem:
At the end of a day shift, an FY1 doctor hands over a 76-year-old man admitted with an upper gastrointestinal bleed to the night medical team. Over the last hour he has become more tachycardic and his blood pressure is falling.

Which information is most important to include?

options.A: His name, bed number and named consultant
options.B: His full past history and complete medication list
options.C: A copy of the admission clerking for the night team to read
options.D: His latest observations and the morning's blood results
options.E: His current condition, the main concerns, treatment given so far and the specific tasks and escalation plan still needed

correct_answer: E. His current condition, the main concerns, treatment given so far and the specific tasks and escalation plan still needed
why_correct: Handover of an unstable patient must allow the receiving team to act safely straight away. The key elements are his current clinical status and trend, what is worrying the team, what has already been done, and what still needs doing, including when to escalate, for example to endoscopy or critical care. A structured format such as SBAR helps ensure nothing important is missed.
why_wrong: A. Identifiers alone give no clinical information. B. Background is relevant but does not tell the night team what to do now. C. Reading a clerking takes time and omits current developments. D. Results without interpretation, concerns or a plan are incomplete.
pearl: Handover should be face to face or by phone where possible for unwell patients, supported by a written record.
thinking: Patient deteriorating ↓ Night team must act immediately ↓ Status, concerns, actions taken ↓ Outstanding tasks and escalation plan ↓ Use a structured format
exam_trap: D, Latest observations and bloods — data feel concrete, but without the concerns, treatment given and plan, the night team cannot act effectively.
takeaway: For a deteriorating patient, hand over status, concerns, treatment given and outstanding actions with an escalation plan.

stem:
A hospital policy states that every inpatient with diabetes should have a foot examination within 24 hours of admission. The diabetes team reviews notes for a sample of patients to see how often this happened, compares the result with the policy, introduces a teaching session and a prompt on the admission proforma, and then plans to measure again.

What kind of activity is this?

options.A: Prospective cohort study
options.B: Clinical audit
options.C: Randomised controlled trial
options.D: Qualitative research
options.E: Laboratory-based research

correct_answer: B. Clinical audit
why_correct: Clinical audit measures current practice against an agreed standard, implements change where practice falls short, and then re-measures to see whether care has improved. Here the standard is the hospital policy, compliance is measured, changes are made and re-audit is planned, completing the audit cycle. Audit does not generate new knowledge, which distinguishes it from research.
why_wrong: A. A cohort study follows groups over time to study exposures and outcomes. C. There is no random allocation of patients to interventions. D. Qualitative research explores experiences through interviews or focus groups. E. No laboratory work is involved.
pearl: Audit asks whether we are doing what we should be doing; research asks what we should be doing.
thinking: Defined standard exists ↓ Practice measured against it ↓ Changes introduced ↓ Re-measurement planned ↓ This is the audit cycle
exam_trap: A, Prospective cohort study — data are collected on a group of patients, but there is no comparison of exposures and outcomes, only measurement against a standard.
takeaway: Comparing practice against a set standard, changing and re-measuring is clinical audit.

stem:
An emergency department team wants to shorten the time it takes for older patients with hip fractures to receive pain relief. They trial a nurse-initiated analgesia protocol for one week, review the results, tweak the protocol, and then test it again in further short cycles, refining it each time.

What does this approach represent?

options.A: Epidemiological surveillance
options.B: Quality improvement using plan-do-study-act cycles
options.C: Randomised controlled trial
options.D: Case-control study
options.E: Population screening programme

correct_answer: B. Quality improvement using plan-do-study-act cycles
why_correct: Quality improvement uses repeated small-scale tests of change, measuring the effect each time and adapting the intervention, typically through plan-do-study-act cycles. This team is testing, studying and refining its protocol iteratively to improve a process of care. The aim is local improvement rather than generating generalisable research evidence.
why_wrong: A. Surveillance monitors disease or events in a population without testing changes. C. No patients are randomly allocated. D. A case-control study compares people with and without an outcome to look at past exposures. E. Screening identifies unrecognised disease in a healthy population.
pearl: Run charts plotting a measure over time are a common way of showing whether changes in a quality improvement project are having an effect.
thinking: Clear aim to improve a process ↓ Small change tested ↓ Results measured ↓ Change adapted and retested ↓ Iterative PDSA cycles: quality improvement
exam_trap: C, Randomised controlled trial — an intervention is being tested, but there is no randomisation or control group, only repeated cycles of change.
takeaway: Repeated small tests of change with measurement and refinement describe quality improvement using PDSA cycles.

stem:
A practice nurse in a GP surgery has just given a 70-year-old man his intramuscular vaccine. The sharps bin is on a trolley beside her, and she reaches for the needle cap out of habit.

What is the correct action?

options.A: Do not resheathe; dispose of the needle and syringe straight into the sharps bin at the point of use
options.B: Resheathe the needle carefully using both hands
options.C: Bend the needle so it cannot be reused
options.D: Place the uncapped needle in the clinical waste bag
options.E: Leave it on the tray and clear up after the next patient

correct_answer: A. Do not resheathe; dispose of the needle and syringe straight into the sharps bin at the point of use
why_correct: Resheathing used needles is a common cause of needlestick injury. Used sharps should be disposed of immediately by the person who used them, into a sharps container at the point of use, without recapping, bending or breaking the needle. This reduces the risk of blood-borne virus transmission to staff.
why_wrong: B. Two-handed recapping is a well-known cause of needlestick injuries. C. Bending or breaking needles increases injury risk. D. Waste bags can be pierced, endangering staff who handle them. E. Leaving sharps lying around exposes others to injury.
pearl: After a needlestick injury, encourage the wound to bleed, wash it with soap and running water, and report it promptly so the need for post-exposure prophylaxis can be assessed.
thinking: Used needle after injection ↓ Recapping causes needlestick injuries ↓ Sharps bin at point of use ↓ User disposes of their own sharps immediately ↓ Do not recap, bend or leave lying
exam_trap: B, Careful two-handed resheathing — it feels tidy and safe, but recapping is exactly how many needlestick injuries happen.
takeaway: Never recap used needles; dispose of them immediately into a sharps container at the point of use.

stem:
An FY2 doctor visiting a nursing home finishes examining one resident's chest and moves on to the resident in the next room. She plans to put on a fresh pair of gloves instead of cleaning her hands, as her hands look clean.

What is the main reason hand hygiene is needed at this point?

options.A: It is only really needed before aseptic procedures
options.B: Putting on new gloves makes hand hygiene unnecessary
options.C: It reduces the spread of microorganisms from one resident to the next
options.D: It mainly protects the doctor from catching an infection
options.E: It is only needed when hands are visibly dirty

correct_answer: C. It reduces the spread of microorganisms from one resident to the next
why_correct: Hands are the main route by which microorganisms are carried between patients, so hand hygiene before and after each patient contact is a key measure to prevent healthcare-associated infection. Hands can be contaminated even when they look clean. Gloves do not replace hand hygiene, as hands can become contaminated through tiny defects and when gloves are removed.
why_wrong: A. Hand hygiene is needed before and after every patient contact, not only for aseptic tasks. B. Gloves are not a substitute; hands should be cleaned before putting them on and after removing them. D. Its main purpose is protecting patients, although it also protects staff. E. Visible soiling is not required for transmission to occur.
pearl: Alcohol hand rub is not effective against Clostridioides difficile spores or norovirus, so soap and water is needed in those situations.
thinking: Moving between residents ↓ Hands carry organisms even when they look clean ↓ Gloves are not a substitute ↓ Hand hygiene before and after each contact ↓ Prevents cross-infection
exam_trap: B, Using fresh gloves instead — it seems equivalent, but gloves do not remove contamination already on the hands and may leak.
takeaway: Clean hands before and after every patient contact to prevent cross-infection, even when gloves are used.

stem:
On a surgical ward, an FY1 doctor adjusts the infusion pump settings and moves the bedside table out of the way. She then turns to palpate the abdomen of a 68-year-old man who had a bowel resection two days ago.

Which step is most important at this point to protect the patient from infection?

options.A: Put on a pair of non-sterile gloves straight away
options.B: Clean her hands thoroughly once the abdominal examination is finished
options.C: Wipe down the infusion pump with a detergent wipe
options.D: Wash her hands at the sink when the ward round ends
options.E: Decontaminate her hands with alcohol rub before touching him

correct_answer: E. Decontaminate her hands with alcohol rub before touching him
why_correct: Touching the pump and furniture will have contaminated her hands with organisms from the patient environment. Cleaning hands immediately before touching the patient is the first of the WHO five moments for hand hygiene and stops those organisms reaching a vulnerable post-operative patient. Alcohol hand rub is suitable as her hands are not visibly soiled.
why_wrong: A. Gloves put on over contaminated hands still carry organisms and do not replace hand hygiene. B. Hand hygiene afterwards protects others, not this patient from what is already on her hands. C. Cleaning equipment does nothing for the organisms already on her hands. D. Hands must be cleaned at each patient contact, not deferred to the end of the round.
pearl: Alcohol hand rub is adequate for most moments, but soap and water are needed when hands are visibly soiled or when caring for patients with diarrhoea such as suspected Clostridioides difficile, because alcohol does not kill spores.
thinking: Hands touched equipment and the bed space ↓ Environment carries organisms ↓ About to touch the patient ↓ WHO moment one: before patient contact ↓ Clean hands now, before examining
exam_trap: A, Putting on gloves — it feels protective, but gloves pulled on over contaminated hands transfer organisms to the patient and never replace hand hygiene.
takeaway: Clean your hands immediately before touching a patient, even when you are about to put on gloves.

stem:
In a busy GP surgery, a practice nurse finishes dressing a leg ulcer for a 79-year-old woman and removes her gloves. Her next task is to take blood from a man waiting in the same room.

What should she do before moving on?

options.A: Go straight to the next patient because she wore gloves throughout
options.B: Clean her hands only if they look soiled after removing the gloves
options.C: Perform hand hygiene now, after this patient contact and glove removal
options.D: Put a fresh pair of gloves on without cleaning her hands
options.E: Leave hand washing until the end of the morning clinic

correct_answer: C. Perform hand hygiene now, after this patient contact and glove removal
why_correct: Hands become contaminated during patient contact and while removing gloves, which can also have small unseen perforations. Hand hygiene after touching a patient and after glove removal is one of the WHO five moments and prevents organisms being carried to the next patient or the environment.
why_wrong: A. Wearing gloves does not mean the hands underneath are clean. B. Hands can carry organisms without looking dirty. D. New gloves over contaminated hands still allow cross-transmission. E. Delaying until the end of the clinic allows organisms to pass between patients.
pearl: Glove removal is a recognised moment of hand contamination, so hand hygiene is always required immediately after taking gloves off.
thinking: Patient contact just finished ↓ Gloves removed, hands possibly contaminated ↓ Next patient is waiting ↓ WHO moment: after patient contact ↓ Clean hands before moving on
exam_trap: B, Cleaning only if visibly soiled — it seems efficient, but organisms are invisible and hands must be cleaned after every patient contact.
takeaway: Always clean your hands after touching a patient and after removing gloves, before anything else.

stem:
A healthcare assistant in a care home tells the visiting doctor that she does not bother cleaning her hands between residents because she always wears gloves when helping them wash.

Which statement should the doctor use to correct her?

options.A: Gloves give complete protection, so her current practice is acceptable
options.B: Gloves can be kept on between residents provided they are not torn
options.C: Hand hygiene is needed only before aseptic procedures, not personal care
options.D: Double gloving would remove the need for hand hygiene
options.E: Hand hygiene is still required before putting gloves on and after taking them off

correct_answer: E. Hand hygiene is still required before putting gloves on and after taking them off
why_correct: Gloves are not a substitute for hand hygiene. They can have tiny perforations, and hands are commonly contaminated when gloves are removed. Hands must therefore be cleaned before gloves are put on and after they are taken off, and gloves must be changed between residents and tasks.
why_wrong: A. Gloves reduce but do not eliminate contamination of the hands. B. Gloves are single use and must be changed between residents. C. Hand hygiene applies to all patient contact, including personal care. D. Extra gloves still leave hands contaminated on removal.
pearl: Gloves should be worn only when there is a risk of contact with blood, body fluids, mucous membranes or non-intact skin; unnecessary glove use increases cross-infection and skin damage.
thinking: Carer relies on gloves alone ↓ Gloves can leak and hands are contaminated on removal ↓ Gloves are single use per resident and task ↓ Hand hygiene before and after gloves ↓ Correct her practice
exam_trap: B, Keeping intact gloves on between residents — it sounds economical, but gloves carry organisms from one person to the next and must be changed and hands cleaned each time.
takeaway: Gloves never replace hand hygiene; clean hands before putting them on and after taking them off.
